The `kernel-obs` package installs the `kernel-obs` upatch and the
`userns-unshare-counter` upatch. `kernel-obs` provides host
observability for executed programs, network peers and volumes,
listeners, DNS answers, watched destinations, privilege transitions
and access to credential and persistence files. Every hook observes;
nothing in this package enforces. `userns-unshare-counter` counts calls
to `unshare()` that request a new user namespace; it does not block or
change them. Its `userns_unshare_calls` per-CPU map holds the count.

Each table lives in one BPF arena and holds one export interval: the
export flips to a fresh buffer, drains the previous one and clears it,
so a table never fills up for good and every snapshot reports the
allocations it had to refuse (`interval.overflow`) and records a
previous, unfinished export left behind (`interval.lost`). Records are
per-interval deltas with first- and last-seen wall-clock timestamps.

Run installation and map commands on the target. The target needs
shirudo initialized before loading the package.

Use the package reference supplied by your publisher:

```sh
PACKAGE=oci://quay.io/namespace/kernel-obs:0.0.1
shirudo bpm key fingerprint "$PACKAGE"
```

Compare the printed SHA-256 public-key fingerprint with the one the
publisher gave you through a trusted channel and proceed only when they
match. For first-time target setup, import the verified certificate
before initializing shirudo:

```sh
sudo shirudo bpm key add "$PACKAGE"
sudo shirudo bpm key list
```

```sh
sudo shirudo bpm install "$PACKAGE"
sudo shirudo upatch list
```

`shirudo bpm info "$PACKAGE"` prints this document without installing.

The Beefile has a tree entry for `kernel-obs`, without a selector, so
a signed upatch tree can take it and every node that syncs the tree
loads it. `userns-unshare-counter` has none and reaches a node with
`bpm install` alone:

```sh
shirudo bpm tree append kernel-obs-<version>.bee oci://<registry>/<tree> --keys-dir <keys>
```

| Map | Key | Records |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `exec` | executable, calling image, cgroup, euid | name, resolved path, uid, effective capabilities, pid, exec count; scripts yield one record for the script and a flagged one for the interpreter |
| `net` | executable, cgroup, protocol, role, peer address and port | connects or datagrams sent, packets and bytes in each direction, pid; accepted and listener-side peers aggregate by address, without the ephemeral port |
| `socket` | creator and current caller, family, type, protocol and operation | socket creation attempts for every family, plus bind/connect/listen/accept/send/receive/option/shutdown activity for IP, packet, XDP, UNIX, NETLINK and VSOCK sockets |
| `listen` | executable, cgroup, protocol, local address and port | TCP listens and UDP binds to a fixed port, with backlog |
| `watch` | executable, cgroup, protocol, destination | attempts and packets towards addresses in `watch.list` |
| `dns` | executable, cgroup, answered address | up to four names that resolved to the address, with counts |
| `priv` | executable, cgroup, kind, subtype, euid | setuid to root, root without an exec or setuid to explain it, ptrace attach, mount

To inspect the unshare counter, use `shirudo upatch map
userns-unshare-counter userns_unshare_calls`. Running `unshare -U true`
triggers the traced path.

, executable mmap and mprotect requests, kernel file and module loads, user namespace creation, bpf() use |
| `file` | executable, cgroup, euid, open mode, path | opens matching `file-watch.list`, with the filesystem magic |
| `watch_stat` | per-CPU counters | metric: socket-level checks against the watch list and matches |

Records include first- and last-seen timestamps and available task
identity. Executable identity is `{dev, ino}` with a cgroup id. Socket
records keep separate `owner` and `actor` identities with known and
inferred flags. Other tables flag a task that started before the upatch
loaded as `caller_inferred` when its mapped executable is first observed.

The `mmap_exec` privilege records report mapping requests that include
`PROT_EXEC`; `mprotect_exec` records transitions that newly grant it.
Their subtype is the requested protection bits; `mmap_exec` stores
mapping flags in `aux`, while `mprotect_exec` stores the VMA length.
`name` is the backing file name or `anonymous`. These hooks observe
requests, not whether the mapping succeeds or code runs.

Socket records describe attempts at the LSM hook; byte counts are
requested send or receive lengths, not confirmed transfers. Socket type
flags such as `SOCK_CLOEXEC` and `SOCK_NONBLOCK` are stripped before the
creation hook, so records retain the base type. Families without detailed
operation hooks still get creation, family, type and protocol records.
Sockets already open when the upatch loads are not enumerated; their owner
is marked inferred when an operation is first observed. Kernel-space
creations are not recorded. UNIX paths, message payloads and VSOCK peer
identifiers are not recorded. AF_PACKET and AF_XDP ring records cover setup
and wakeup calls, not individual frames.

DNS records keep the question name of the query an answer resolved, its
labels joined by dots. A label may hold any byte; a NUL, a dot, a space
or any other byte outside printable ASCII in it is recorded as `?`, so
that the recorded name keeps the length and the labels of the name
queried. The labels `www.good` and `example` are recorded as
`www?good.example`, not as the three labels of `www.good.example`, and
`ww\0w.evil.example`, whose first label holds a NUL, as
`ww?w.evil.example` rather than `ww`.

Packet counts come from the cgroup hooks on the root cgroup and cover
every socket on the host, including sockets created before the load,
which are attributed to their cgroup alone until their owner is known.
Packets are counted as the socket layer sees them, before segmentation
offload splits them on the wire.

`watch.list` holds IPv4 and IPv6 addresses or prefixes; attempts to
reach them are recorded in `watch` in addition to `net`. The shipped
list names the cloud instance metadata addresses and the public
DNS-over-HTTPS resolvers. `file-watch.list` holds base names,
`parent/name` pairs or `parent/*` directory rules, optionally with a
trailing `w` for opens for writing only. Both are compiled into the
signed object: edit the list, run `make lists` in this directory and
rebuild the package. There is nothing to configure on the target.

To update only the watch addresses in an existing `.upatch`, run
`python3 rewrite_watch_upatch.py watch.list kernel-obs.upatch`. It takes
the same address and CIDR format as `gen_watch.py`, preserves the compiled
loader and BTF, and re-signs the changed `.rodata` with the operator key
from `/var/lib/shirudo/keys` (or `--keys-dir`). Use `--dry-run` to check
that the new tries fit the arrays in the existing BTF layout, or `-o` to
write a separate artifact. The tool refuses a list that needs more trie
nodes than the existing arrays hold; changing those capacities still
requires rebuilding the BPF object.

The Beefile also declares `watch.list` as the input for both watch trie
variables. `bpm build` uses `gen_watch_rodata.py` to create their raw BTF
values. The input name is derived from the basename before its first dot,
so `watch.list` is named `watch`; override it for one build with:

```sh
shirudo bpm build ./upatches/kernel-obs --version 0.1.1 \
	--rodata-input watch=./customer/watch.list
```

To update the data without recompiling BPF, `bpm config update` reads the
Beefile and updater dependencies from a previously built package. This
chooses to trust and run the package's updater on the operator; those files
are not covered by the upatch CMS signature. It then writes a new versioned
package:

```sh
shirudo bpm config update \
	--base-package oci://registry.example.com/shirudo/kernel-obs:0.1.0 \
	--version 0.1.1 \
	--rodata-input watch=./customer/watch.list
```

Pass `-f ./upatches/kernel-obs/Beefile` to use the local Beefile
and updater files instead. The target receives only the newly signed
upatch and never runs the updater.

```sh
sudo shirudo upatch map kernel-obs
sudo shirudo upatch map kernel-obs exec
sudo shirudo upatch map kernel-obs exec --json
sudo shirudo upatch map kernel-obs net --show-full
sudo shirudo upatch map kernel-obs priv --json=./priv.ndjson
```

Reading a table drains it, exactly as the map-export timer does; add
`--peek` to look at the interval being collected without taking it
from the exporter.

`kernel-obs` is written for the preemption model of the kernel the test
VM runs: `CONFIG_PREEMPT_LAZY` alone, without `CONFIG_PREEMPT_DYNAMIC`
and so without preemptible RCU (`CONFIG_PREEMPT_RCU`). The VM suite is
where the package is loaded and its tables are checked, in CI and in a
local `make tests`, so its concurrency is reviewed against the kernel
that suite runs rather than against one no test exercises.

On that kernel the `lsm` and `cgroup_skb` programs run with preemption
disabled, so no other task's run starts on a CPU before one ends; a
softirq can still run an ingress program on top of an egress one, and
the sleepable `lsm.s` programs can sleep. The DNS parser builds a query
in a per-CPU scratch buffer without a guard: only egress runs use it,
and those come from the task that sends the query, so on that kernel
none starts before another ends. Runs on different CPUs share the arena
tables on every kernel, so the tables take and count their entries with
atomics, publish a buffer with a release store, and an export expects
late writes into the buffer it drains.

A kernel with preemptible RCU, which `CONFIG_PREEMPT`,
`CONFIG_PREEMPT_RT` and `CONFIG_PREEMPT_DYNAMIC` bring, is outside that
model. `PREEMPT_DYNAMIC` is the kernel's default and what distribution
kernels use, and since 7.0 it boots only in its `full` or `lazy` mode;
before, distribution kernels mostly booted it as `voluntary`, which does
not preempt a running program. On such a kernel another task's egress
run can preempt a DNS query parse on the same CPU and overwrite the
scratch, so that a DNS record carries the name of another query. The
record is wrong, nothing more: `kernel-obs` observes and decides
nothing.

DNS over TCP, TLS and HTTPS is not parsed; the resolvers are on the
watch list instead, and DNS on ports other than 53 is not looked at.
IPv6 extension headers are not walked. Forwarded traffic does not pass
the cgroup hooks and is not counted.

The `app-sandbox` package installs the `app-sandbox` upatch, which puts
applications in sandboxes. A sandbox restricts every task that executed
one of its files, and the tasks those start, in three things:

- what it executes: its own files and those of the policies it names;
- where it connects and sends: the networks it names;
- which files it creates, renames and opens for writing or truncates:
  none whose name matches a pattern it denies.

The package ships sandboxes for Apache httpd and PHP-FPM that keep a web
application from writing the PHP files it serves, from starting other
programs and from reaching beyond private networks: what an attacker
who found a hole in the application does first. Replace them with
sandboxes for your own applications.

Its tree entry names the PHP2Shell advisories, CVE-2026-109618 and
CVE-2026-109619, as `fixes`, so that a backend that reads the tree
counts a node that loaded the upatch as shielded against them. The
sandboxes do not close the hole in PHP: a request can still run the
attacker's code in the application. They keep that code from leaving a
PHP file behind, from running another program and from connecting out.
Upgrade PHP as well.

A sandbox restricts and never grants: a task in it keeps every limit it
had. It is not a boundary against root outside the sandbox, and a file
replaced after the load is a new file without the label, see "Limits".

A sandbox has two parts. The `Beefile` gives it a name, a policy bit and
the executables that put a task in it, as a `[[upatches.policy]]` table
(see `Documentation/reference/formats/beefile.rst`):

```toml
[[upatches.policy]]
id = "apache"
bit = 0x1
paths = ["/usr/sbin/apache2", "/usr/sbin/httpd"]
```

The last component of a path may be a pattern, as in
`/usr/sbin/php-fpm*` for the PHP-FPM of any version: the target labels
every regular file of the directory that matches it.

`sandbox.toml` gives the rules of the sandbox of that name:

```toml
[networks]
localnet = ["127.0.0.0/8", "10.0.0.0/8", "::1/128"]

[sandbox.apache]
exec = ["apache-helpers"]
network = ["@localnet", "192.0.2.10/32"]

[sandbox.apache.deny]
create = ["*.php"]
rename = ["*.php"]
write = ["*.php"]
```

| Key | Without it | With it |
|---|---|---|
| `exec` | The task executes anything. | It executes only files labeled with its own policy or with one of the policy IDs listed, each a `[[upatches.policy]]` table of the Beefile. `exec = []` allows its own files alone. |
| `network` | The task connects anywhere. | It connects and sends only to the networks listed, IPv4 or IPv6 in CIDR form, or `@<name>` for a list of `[networks]`. An IPv4 network also covers its IPv4-mapped IPv6 form. It creates no raw and no packet socket. `network = []` allows no IP peer. |
| `deny.create` | | It creates no file, directory, device, symbolic link or hard link with a matching name. |
| `deny.rename` | | It renames no file from or to a matching name. |
| `deny.write` | | It opens no file with a matching name for writing and does not truncate one. |

A pattern is matched against the last component of the path. It is the
name itself, or holds one `*` for any run of bytes, and `?` for any one
byte, with at most 32 bytes on each side of the `*`.

A script is executed with its interpreter, and the kernel asks for
both: a sandbox with `exec` runs a script only when the script and its
interpreter are each labeled with a policy the sandbox allows.

The package holds up to 32 sandboxes with `exec`, 128 networks and 64
patterns. A task in two sandboxes, one that executed files of both, is
held to the rules of each.

`gen_policy.py` turns `sandbox.toml` into the `sandbox_policy` variable
of the upatch when `shirudo bpm build` runs, and fails the build for a
sandbox the Beefile declares no policy for, a network or a pattern it
cannot read and a table it does not know. Read back what a build holds
with:

```sh
shirudo bpm info data app-sandbox-<version>.bee upatches/app-sandbox.upatch
```

Build in a directory that holds shirudo's BPF headers and a `vmlinux.h`
(see `Documentation/start/guides/publish-package.rst`):

```sh
shirudo bpm build upatches/app-sandbox --version 1.0.0 --keys-dir <keys>
shirudo bpm push app-sandbox-1.0.0.bee oci://<registry>/<namespace>/app-sandbox --keys-dir <keys>
shirudo bpm tree append app-sandbox-1.0.0.bee oci://<registry>/<tree> --keys-dir <keys>
```

The Beefile has a tree entry without a selector, with the advisories
above as its `fixes`, so every node that syncs the tree loads the
upatch; on a node without the applications it labels nothing and
restricts nothing. Add a selector to load it only where they run:

```toml
[upatches.tree.selector.labels]
role = ["web"]
```

`tools/put-shields`, and `make shields` with it, publishes the package
with the other shields of `upatches/`.

`--rodata-input sandbox=<file>` builds with other rules for the
policies of the Beefile, and `shirudo bpm config update` signs new rules
into a package already built, without compiling it again.

The load labels each path of the Beefile that exists on the target with
its policy bit, in the `security.bpf.shirudo.policy` xattr. shirudo
gives a task the bits of every file it executes, and its children
inherit them, so a task enters a sandbox at its next `execve()` of a
labeled file: restart the application after the first load. An unload
leaves the labels, which restrict nothing once the upatch is gone.

Every refusal is `EACCES`.

`demo/` in the source of this package holds a web server to try the
`apache` sandbox on: Apache httpd with PHP from the official
`php:8.4-apache` image, a site on port 8443 and `attack.php`, which
does from inside PHP what an attacker would next. `demo/build.sh` writes
the image's file system to an archive, and `demo/apache.sh` unpacks it
on a target and runs Apache from it in a chroot, with `/usr/sbin/apache2`
a hard link to its binary. `Documentation/start/guides/system-hardening.rst`
walks through it.

- A path that does not exist at the load is not labeled, and a file
  that replaces a labeled one, as a package upgrade does, is a new file
  without the label, whether a path or a pattern named it. Load the upatch again after the application is
  installed or upgraded.
- The file rules name files, not their contents: a descriptor that was
  open for writing before the task entered the sandbox, or that another
  process passes to it, still writes.
- The network rules cover `connect()` and the address of `sendmsg()`
  and `sendto()` on IPv4 and IPv6 sockets. Other address families pass,
  and so does what a task receives or accepts.
- Root outside a sandbox can remove nothing of it, as only shirudo's
  runtime sets the label, but a task that root starts from an unlabeled
  file is in no sandbox.

The programs keep no state of their own: they read the task's policy
bits and the rules, which never change after the load, so they are
right on every preemption model.

A task in no sandbox pays one task-storage lookup at each hook, and
none when it opens a file for reading. The hooks are the LSM hooks of
`execve()`, `connect()`, `sendmsg()`, `socket()`, the creation, linking
and renaming of a directory entry, an open for writing and a change of
size. A task in a sandbox pays a scan of the rules on top: at most 128
networks, or 64 patterns of at most 64 bytes.

What ``shirudo upatch map --otel`` and ``shirudo upatch map --all``
export from a upatch's maps: a log record or the decoder's metrics per
map, a reference to a snapshot stored in S3, or a line of JSON. The
transport, the endpoint and the resource it shares with the keepalive
are in :doc:`otlp`.

One log record per map:

.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 1
   :widths: 30 70

* - Field
     - Value
   * - ``timeUnixNano``, ``observedTimeUnixNano``
     - Wall clock when shirudo builds the document, nanoseconds since
       the epoch, decimal string.
   * - ``severityNumber``, ``severityText``
     - ``9``, ``INFO``
   * - ``eventName``
     - ``shirudo.bpf.map.snapshot``
   * - ``body``
     - The value the map's decoder returns, as an OTLP value. Without a
       decoder, a ``kvlistValue`` of the map's contents, see
       `Undecoded body`_.
   * - Attribute ``shirudo.upatch.name``
     - The upatch name.
   * - Attribute ``shirudo.upatch.location``
     - The upatch's attach point.
   * - Attribute ``shirudo.map.name``
     - The map name.
   * - Attribute ``shirudo.map.type``
     - The map type name.
   * - Attribute ``shirudo.map.max_entries``
     - Integer.
   * - Attribute ``shirudo.map.n_entries``
     - Integer, entries read.
   * - Attribute ``shirudo.map.n_cpus``
     - Integer.
   * - Attribute ``shirudo.map.serialized``
     - Boolean, the map was read through its serializer.
   * - Attribute ``shirudo.map.truncated``
     - Boolean, the read stopped before the last entry.

A decoded body larger than ``map_export.log_record_max_bytes`` (default
1048576, at most ``map_export.otlp_max_bytes``) fails with ``E2BIG``.

.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 1
   :widths: 30 70

* - Key
     - Value
   * - ``name``, ``type``, ``max_entries``, ``n_entries``
     - The map.
   * - ``n_cpus``
     - Per-CPU maps only.
   * - ``serialized``
     - Boolean.
   * - ``serialized_pages``, ``serialized_bytes``, ``pages``
     - Serializer-backed maps. Each page has ``page_index``,
       ``cursor``, ``next_cursor``, ``done``, ``flags``, ``chunks``,
       ``bytes`` and ``data_hex``.
   * - ``skipped``
     - The reason, for a map type shirudo cannot read generically.
   * - ``truncated``, ``n_truncated_at``
     - Other maps. ``n_truncated_at`` only when truncated.
   * - ``btf``
     - ``key_type``, ``value_type``, and ``key_type_def`` and
       ``value_type_def`` when known.
   * - ``entries``
     - Each with ``key`` and ``value``, or for per-CPU maps ``key``,
       ``values_per_cpu`` and ``sum``, formatted from BTF.

A decoder that declares the metric signal returns a list of OTLP
``Metric`` objects. shirudo sends them as
``resourceMetrics[0].scopeMetrics[0].metrics`` under the resource and
scope of :ref:`otlp-resource-scope` and adds no attributes.

.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 1
   :widths: 40 60

* - Map
     - Export
   * - Has a decoder
     - The signal the decoder declares, log or metric.
   * - No decoder, unsigned per-CPU integer value
     - Classified as a metric. Metrics come only from decoders, so the
       export fails with ``ENODATA``.
   * - No decoder, any other map
     - Log record with the undecoded body.

For an undecoded map ``upatch map`` prints the choice on standard
error as ``otel: selected <signal> for <type> map <name>: <reason>``.

* - Property
     - Value
   * - URI
     - ``s3://<bucket>[/<prefix>]``. Bucket: 3 to 63 characters from
       ``a-z``, ``0-9``, ``.`` and ``-``, starting and ending with a
       letter or digit. Prefix: at most 512 bytes, no control
       characters, ``?``, ``#``, ``.`` or ``..`` segments.
   * - Object
     - The decoder's JSON output, gzip-compressed, at most 64 MiB
       before compression.
   * - Key
     - ``[<prefix>/]<host>/<upatch>/<map>/<sha256>.json.gz``.
       ``<host>`` is the host name with every character other than
       ``A-Z``, ``a-z``, ``0-9``, ``-``, ``_`` and ``.`` replaced by
       ``_``. ``<sha256>`` is the digest of the compressed object.
   * - URL
     - With ``AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3``: ``<endpoint>/<bucket>/<key>``.
       Else ``https://<bucket>.s3.<region>.amazonaws.com/<key>``, or
       ``https://s3.<region>.amazonaws.com/<bucket>/<key>`` for a
       bucket name with a dot.
   * - Request
     - ``PUT`` signed with AWS SigV4, with ``If-None-Match: *``,
       ``Cache-Control: immutable``, ``x-amz-content-sha256``,
       ``x-amz-checksum-sha256``, ``x-amz-meta-shirudo-schema: 1``,
       ``x-amz-meta-shirudo-upatch`` and ``x-amz-meta-shirudo-map

When a decoded map's document fails with ``E2BIG`` and an S3 URI is
set (``--s3-uri=<uri>`` or ``map_export.s3_uri``), shirudo uploads the
snapshot to S3 and sends a reference log record instead. Undecoded,
skipped and truncated maps are not uploaded.
``map_export.s3_uri`` requires ``map_export.otel_endpoint``.

.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 1
   :widths: 30 70

``.
       ``412`` counts as already uploaded.
   * - Timeout and retries
     - 10 seconds per attempt. Retries as for OTLP, also on ``408``,
       ``409`` and ``500``.
   * - Cleartext
     - As for OTLP, for ``AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3``. Insecure mode also
       turns off certificate verification for the AWS endpoints.

.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 1
   :widths: 40 60

* - Variable
     - Value
   * - ``AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID``, ``AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY``
     - Required. Missing credentials fail with ``EACCES``.
   * - ``AWS_SESSION_TOKEN``
     - Sent as ``x-amz-security-token``.
   * - ``AWS_REGION``, ``AWS_DEFAULT_REGION``
     - Region, in this order, default ``us-east-1``.
   * - ``AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3``
     - S3-compatible endpoint, path-style.
   * - ``AWS_CA_BUNDLE``
     - CA bundle for the S3 endpoint.

The reference log record goes to the logs endpoint, whatever signal
the decoder declares, and is not subject to
``map_export.otlp_max_bytes``:

.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 1
   :widths: 44 56

* - Field
     - Value
   * - ``eventName``
     - ``shirudo.bpf.map.snapshot.reference``
   * - ``severityNumber``, ``severityText``
     - ``9``, ``INFO``
   * - ``body``
     - ``stringValue``: ``BPF map snapshot stored in S3: <uri>``
   * - Attributes
     - The map snapshot attributes above, and
       ``shirudo.map.snapshot.uri``,
       ``shirudo.map.snapshot.format`` (``shirudo.map.v1+json``),
       ``shirudo.map.snapshot.content_type`` (``application/json``),
       ``shirudo.map.snapshot.content_encoding`` (``gzip``),
       ``shirudo.map.snapshot.size_bytes``,
       ``shirudo.map.snapshot.uncompressed_size_bytes`` and
       ``shirudo.map.snapshot.sha256``.

``map_export.json_path`` or ``upatch map --json=<path>`` appends one line
per map to a file, instead of OTLP or besides it. The line is the JSON
value the map's decoder returns, not an OTLP document. A map without a
decoder fails with ``ENODATA``. ``map_export.json_path`` must be an
absolute path. A file or directory that carries shirudo's seal label is
refused. A new file gets mode ``0644``.

List the pinned maps of the loaded upatches, print one map's contents, or
export maps as JSON lines, OTLP or S3 objects.

Runs on: target, as root with the runtime binary. Requires: loaded
upatches with pinned maps. Changes measured state: no.

.. code-block:: none

shirudo upatch map [<upatch>] [--json | --json=<path>]
   shirudo upatch map <upatch> <map> [--json | --json=<path>] [--show-full] [--peek]
                      [--otel [--otel-endpoint=<url>] [--tenant-id=<id>]
                              [--otel-insecure] [--otel-retries=<retries>]
                              [--s3-uri=<uri>]]
   shirudo upatch map --all [--json | --json=<path>] [--show-full] [--peek]
                      [--otel [<otlp-options>]]

``--json`` takes its path after ``=`` only. The other options with a
value take it after ``=`` or as the next argument.

Without arguments, ``map`` lists every pinned map of every loaded upatch
with its type and maximum number of entries. With ``<upatch>``, it lists the maps of that
upatch. ``--json`` prints the list as ``{"schema":1,"maps":[...]}`` with
``upatch``, ``name``, ``type``, ``max_entries`` and, for a per-CPU map,
``n_cpus`` per map.

With ``<upatch> <map>``, ``map`` reads the map:

- A map is decoded through its BTF types when the build kept them
  (``shirudo build`` compiles with ``-g``).
- When the upatch pins a serializer program for the map, ``map`` runs it
  and prints the pages it returns. Such a read drains the serializer:
  records it returns are gone for the next reader, the export timer
  included. ``--peek`` reads the interval being collected without taking
  it.
- The human output shows at most 256 entries unless ``--show-full``.
  JSON and OTLP output have no limit.
- ``--json`` prints one JSON line to standard output. ``--json=<path>``
  appends it to ``<path>``.
- ``--otel`` sends the map to an OTLP collector. A map with a signed Lua
  decoder is sent as the log or metric the decoder declares. A map
  without one is classified by shirudo (see
  :doc:`/reference/formats/map-export`).

``--all`` handles every map of every loaded upatch as above and loads the
``map_export`` settings (:doc:`/reference/configuration`):
``map_export.json_path`` turns on JSON output to that file and
``map_export.otel_endpoint`` turns on OTLP, together with the tenant,
TLS, retry, size and S3 settings. Options on the command line take
precedence.

With neither a JSON nor an OTLP destination, ``--all`` prints every map in
full detail on standard output, draining every serializer-backed map
unless ``--peek``. ``shirudo-map-export.timer`` runs ``upatch map --all``
every five seconds, so without a configured destination it drains the
maps into the journal.

* - Option
     - Argument
     - Default
     - Description
   * - ``--all``
     - none
     - off
     - Handle every map of every loaded upatch. Takes no positional
       argument.
   * - ``--json``
     - optional ``<path>`` after ``=``
     - off
     - Print JSON, or append it to ``<path>``.
   * - ``--show-full``
     - none
     - off
     - Lift the 256-entry limit of the human output.
   * - ``--peek``

   * - ``--otel``

   * - ``--otel-endpoint``

       ``OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_*`` variables, else ``http://localhost:4318``
     - OTLP base URL. The signal path is appended.
   * - ``--tenant-id``
     - ``<id>``, 1 to 128 of ``A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ -``
     - ``map_export.tenant_id`` with ``--all``

:audience: Security reviewers, Operators

shirudo restricts the ``bpf()`` system call so that only loaders signed
with the operator's key install BPF code, root included. Every change to
the set of loaded upatches is measured in the TPM, and an operator
checks that measurement with evidence the TPM signs. This page is the short
version of the :doc:`threat-model`, which states each mechanism, its
limits and the gaps not closed yet.

* - Goal
     - Mechanism
     - Limit
     - Threat model
   * - Only signed BPF enters the kernel
     - ``lsm/bpf`` admits only signed loaders from userspace. The kernel
       verifies them against the sealed ``.bpf`` keyring, and
       ``lsm/bpf_prog_load`` admits only that keyring.
     - Any artifact the key ever signed loads. In-kernel BPF users and
       classic BPF are outside the gate.
     - :ref:`T1 <tm-t1>`, R16, R18
   * - Enforcement stays attached
     - Detach, update and foreign attach commands are refused; pins,
       descriptors and the private bpffs mount are guarded.
     - The pins depend on the mount tree; a stopped runtime command
       keeps its descriptors.
     - :ref:`T2 <tm-t2>`, R3, U17
   * - Only shirudo changes its state
     - The seal labels ``/var/lib/shirudo`` and checks every change to
       a labeled inode; keyrings and authorized processes are guarded.
     - Offline writes bypass it.
     - :ref:`T3 <tm-t3>`, R19
   * - Every change is measured
     - Loads, unloads, revocations and tree operations extend a TPM NV
       register whose writes ``lsm/tpm_command`` keeps to shirudo;
       salted sessions authenticate TPM acknowledgments

.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 1
   :widths: 20 32 30 18

 and readbacks.
     - Initial session-key enrollment trusts the initrd; the config
       PCR is not guarded.
     - :ref:`T5 <tm-t5>`, R4, U9
   * - A verifier can tell
     - ``shirudo attest`` returns a TPM quote and a certification of the
       register; ``shirudo attest verify`` checks them offline.
     - Only the TPM-signed parts are evidence, and only with the
       verifier pinning the key, the binding and the expected state.
     - :ref:`T9 <tm-t9>`, U1
   * - Attempts leave a trace
     - Guards count their refusals in a frozen map that ``shirudo
       status`` and the keepalive report.
     - Some refusals move no counter; telemetry is the target's own
       account.
     - :ref:`T10 <tm-t10>`, R17
   * - Delivered content is authentic
     - Indexes, tree publications and configs are signed; the kernel
       verifies loaders and config roots.
     - A registry can withhold and replay signed content.
     - :ref:`T7 <tm-t7>`, :ref:`T11 <tm-t11>`, R8

The adversary shirudo is built against is root on the target without
the signing key: a compromised administrator account, a container
escape, a persistence implant. Capabilities do not stop it, so shirudo
does not rest on capabilities. A task gains authority only by a
successful exec of a file on the dm-verity runtime image, and the
guards let only such tasks through. Root can still run the runtime binary,
so the command interface is the boundary: root can make shirudo do
anything a shirudo command does, and every such change to the loaded
set is measured.

The other adversaries are unprivileged code, root with mount-namespace
and device control, the network and the registries, a malicious
collector, and the holder of a compromised signing key. The
:ref:`adversaries <tm-adversaries>` section says what each can do.

The properties above hold only on a deployment that provides the
:ref:`assumptions <tm-assumptions>`. In brief:

- A trusted kernel with the BPF LSM, the signed-loader ABI and the
  kernel project patches
- Module signatures, no 32-bit compatibility, no resume device in the
  UKI and no writes under mounted file systems
- Secure Boot with a signed, measured UKI and an authenticated kernel
  command line
- Config signing keys chosen by the authenticated runtime image
- A TPM 2.0 reachable only through the kernel driver
- A runtime image without generic tools
- An operator host that keeps the signing key safe

shirudo checks only some of these. The pre-flight of ``shirudo init``
checks that the BPF LSM is active, that the kernel has the
signed-loader ABI and that it checks module signatures. The target
checks a config's signature against the runtime image's keys itself. It
does not check the rest of the kernel configuration or the boot chain
(U10).

The deployer and the verifier each have a part that no code does for
them. The :ref:`duties <tm-duties>` section lists it in full. The
essentials:

- Build and boot the kernel as :doc:`/operate/plan/hardening` describes.
- Start every shirudo unit from the runtime image, and keep the units'
  environment files empty.
- Verify each target with ``shirudo attest verify`` and always pass
  ``--ak-name``, the binding PCRs, an expected state and the expected
  config root, as :doc:`/operate/run/attest` describes.
- Treat ``shirudo status``, keepalives and tamper counters as the
  target's own account, and a ``tampered`` status as an incident
  (:doc:`/operate/troubleshoot/incident-tampered`).

- :doc:`tamper-counters` for what the counters record
